To transmit electrical energy from renewable resources into a data center, operators use a mix of financial, physical, and grid-level frameworks
and renewable energy is intermittent (the sun doesn't always shine; the wind doesn't always blow), delivering clean power requires sophisticated sourcing models.
The data center remains physically connected to the traditional local utility grid, but its power consumption is financially or contractually tied to a specific renewable energy plant elsewhere.

A financial structure where the data center developer agrees to a fixed price for electricity with a renewable energy developer. The renewable energy is sold directly into the local wholesale market, and the data center receives
to legally offset its carbon footprint.

Local government or state-owned power distribution companies (DISCOMs) offer a specialized "green tariff" tier. The data center pays a premium on its utility bill, and the utility guarantees that it will procure an equivalent amount of renewable energy on the data center's behalf.
The data center physically consumes green energy generated at a distant location by transmitting it across third-party utility lines.

The data center signs a long-term contract to buy electricity from a specific off-site renewable asset (e.g., a solar farm 200 miles away). The power is physically routed through the national or state grid to the data center.

Popular in regions like India, the data center operator sets up a joint-venture equity stake in a renewable power plant (Group Captive). Under open-access regulations, the state grid infrastructure is used to
this power from the generation site directly to the facility, bypassing standard retail utility rates.
To solve the problem of solar dropping off at night or wind dying down, modern providers use a blended approach to provide stable, uninterrupted power.
Combining wind turbines and solar arrays at the same generation site. Wind speeds are often higher at night when solar power is zero, helping smooth out the total generation curve.
A multi-source setup that pairs wind/solar with
. Excess energy generated during peak hours is stored and discharged later, ensuring a steady, constant stream of electricity to match the data center's baseline load.
Power is generated directly on the data center’s property, eliminating transmission lines and utility middle-men entirely.
Photovoltaic (PV) panels installed on the roof of the data center or over parking structures. While this directly feeds clean power into the building, on-site solar usually only covers
of a hyperscale data center's massive power needs.

Emerging technology where hydrogen is stored on-site and converted into electricity via electrochemical reactions, producing only water vapor as a byproduct. These are increasingly used to replace diesel backup generators for emergency outages.

A growing trend for next-generation AI data centers. Operators contract or co-locate with compact, on-site nuclear reactors to get massive, 100% carbon-free, baseline power independent of the weather.
